query: For high-entropy alloys intended for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion, and why? Propose a controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, predict how combined degradation and its wear and corrosion components would differ from a matched baseline, define where the prediction should hold or fail, identify supporting prior evidence, and state an observation that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: High-entropy alloys resist simultaneous wear and corrosion because their inherently homogeneous, single‐phase microstructure promotes the rapid formation and continuous regeneration of a protective, passive oxide (and/or tribolayer) during mechanical damage. This layer minimizes both mechanical abrasion and localized electrochemical attack.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy manufactured as a single-phase, chemically homogeneous microstructure (for example, an equiatomic or optimized formulation such as AlCoCrFeNi or another similarly designed HEA with high configurational entropy).
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to an environment that imposes simultaneous mechanical wear (e.g., reciprocating sliding contact) and exposure to a corrosive medium (e.g., chloride-containing aqueous solution or molten salt).
generation.conditions: Testing at controlled temperatures where passive film formation is thermodynamically favored, with wear load and corrosion conditions set to moderate levels so that the in-situ regeneration of the oxide layer is kinetically viable. A matched baseline (a conventional alloy with lower elemental complexity) is tested under identical conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, adherent passive oxide or tribolayer at the alloy’s surface, whose stability and self-healing capability are mediated by the chemically uniform atomic arrangement and possible short-range order inherent in high-entropy alloys.
generation.mechanism: High configurational entropy suppresses phase segregation and minimizes the formation of localized galvanic cells. Under simultaneous wear, any removed surface is quickly re-oxidized to form a protective layer that acts as a barrier to corrosive species. This dynamic, self-replenishing layer resists both mechanical abrasion and corrosion attack by limiting oxygen and ion ingress.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline alloy of lower complexity, the HEA will show lower combined degradation rates. In tests, the amount of material loss by wear and the depth of corrosion penetration will be reduced, with the combined effect being less than the sum of individual wear and corrosion processes observed in the baseline.
generation.baseline: A structurally and compositionally similar alloy processed to have lower configurational entropy (e.g., a duplex or conventional alloy) that does not form as robust or rapidly regenerating a passive layer under identical wear-corrosion conditions.
generation.boundary: The prediction should hold under conditions where the corrosion medium does not chemically compromise oxide stability and where the wear rate does not exceed the kinetics of re-passivation. In extremely aggressive mechanical wear or environments that dissolve the protective layer faster than it can regenerate, the hypothesis may not hold.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative differences between the HEA and baseline alloys under combined degradation are uncertain and may depend on the specific alloy system, environmental aggressiveness, and details of the passive film chemistry. Further optimization and parameter studies are needed.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one using the high-entropy alloy with a known homogeneous single-phase microstructure and another using a conventional alloy with similar bulk mechanical properties but lower elemental complexity. Expose both sets to a controlled reciprocating sliding wear test in a corrosive medium (e.g., chloride solution) at a temperature that allows passive film formation. Monitor the surface continuously using in-situ microscopy, and perform post-test cross-sectional analysis to assess oxide layer thickness and uniformity.
measurements: Corrosion penetration depth and area (optical/SEM imaging, EDS mapping)
Passive layer composition and thickness (XPS, TEM)
Re-passivation kinetics measured via electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-entropy alloy does not exhibit a significantly lower combined degradation (i.e., if wear-corrosion damage in the HEA is not measurably less than in the conventional alloy) or if no robust, self-healing passive layer is observed (e.g., similar passive layer thickness, composition, or reformation kinetics as the baseline), then the hypothesis is falsified.

A Synergistic Framework for Hardness Prediction and Design of High-Entropy Alloys Based on Deep Learning and Intelligent Optimization Algorithms

Abstract: A synergistic framework combining deep learning with intelligent optimization algorithms has been proposed to predict the hardness and optimize the composition of Al–Ti–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni system high-entropy alloys (HEAs). This forward prediction model systematically refines and selects candidate features through correlation analysis, solid solution strengthening theory, and the NSGA-III algorithm. A hybrid deep learning model integrating transformer attention mechanisms with a multilayer perceptron has been developed, enabling high-accuracy prediction of HEA hardness (R 2 = 0.9813, RMSE = 10.23577). Furthermore, SHAP analysis was employed to investigate the causal links between features and hardness. An inverse design model based on the Egret Swarm Optimization Algorithm was applied to perform reverse optimization of the forward model, achieving optimal compositional combinations for the specified hardness targets. Outstanding radiation resistance of tungsten-based high-entropy alloys

Abstract: Are high-entropy alloys the solution to radiation damage? AbstractA body-centered cubic W-based refractory high entropy alloy with outstanding radiation resistance has been developed. The alloy was grown as thin films showing a bimodal grain size distribution in the nanocrystalline and ultrafine regimes and a unique 4-nm lamella-like structure revealed by atom probe tomography (APT). Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and x-ray diffraction show certain black spots appearing after thermal annealing at elevated temperatures. TEM and APT analysis correlated the black spots with second-phase particles rich in Cr and V. No sign of irradiation-created dislocation loops, even after 8 dpa, was observed. Furthermore, nanomechanical testing shows a large hardness of 14 GPa in the as-deposited samples, with near negligible irradiation hardening. Theoretical modeling combining ab initio and Monte Carlo techniques predicts the formation of Cr- and V-rich second-phase particles and points at equal mobilities of point defects as the origin of the exceptional radiation tolerance.
